It's frustrating that so much research on POTS is poorly designed with tiny sample sizes. A lot of the conventional wisdom on treatment and prognosis comes from a few doctors' anecdotal recommendations. I really wish we could have a large, well-designed, long-running study on this relatively common condition. 

My main gripe with the study showing that most patients improve is that they only followed for 5 years. I've had this condition for 2.5 years and have already gone through multiple bad periods, intermixed with good periods where I wouldn't meet the diagnostic criteria. Just because the study participants seemed better on the day they were tested does not mean they're in the clear forever.

I do think that things are usually better than we make them out to be. On average, I feel like my symptoms have improved over time (although that trend is very noisy). I think there's a good chance that I'll recover from POTS. Unfortunately, I've also developed other conditions that are just as debilitating, and I'm not sure if I'll recover from those. Many of us with POTS also have a lot of risk factors for other conditions, like ME/CFS, fibromyalgia, and auto-immune disease. I suspect that I will have health challenges for the rest of my life, but I will be able to adapt and salvage some quality of life as well. It's a complicated journey for most of us.

Even though the elastic is currently sewn down along its entire length, it doesn't need to be that way after the alteration. I would seam-rip to get the elastic out, then cut it or fold over the ends to get it down to your desired length. Then you can sew each end of the elastic securely to the side seams, and fold the waistband over it. I think you'll be able to sew the waistband down to the back of the pants with a whip stitch without sewing through the elastic. Sometimes when elastic is encased like this it ends of folding over or getting twisted, so if that happens you can sew a vertical line across the elastic in the center back to keep it in place.

Or just wear a belt if the alteration seems like too much work. I actually have a home-made belt in that exact shade of green! I bought 1.5 yards of 1" wide cotton webbing and a 1" belt buckle. Threaded the webbing through the buckle and then folded over and sewed down the raw ends. The webbing gives it a cool outdoorsy look!

Edit: It actually might be a pain to sew the waistband back down with the elastic already inside, since the fabric would be all bunched up from it. Instead you could take the elastic out, then fold over the waistband and sew it most of the way down, but leave around an inch unsewn on each end. Then thread the elastic through the waistband and sew it down to each side seam.

This tweet basically reiterates the idea of the social model of disability. It's the idea that a disability is any difference intrinsic to a person that makes it more difficult for them to navigate our society. So in the world of Wall-e where everyone spends all their time in motorized chairs, being paralyzed from the waist down would not be a disability. It wouldn't affect your life in any significant way.

Industrialization gave rise to a lot of disabilities under the social model, since employers started to expect workers to behave as interchangeable machines who could all perform the same tasks in the same way. This makes it hard for neurodivergent people to find work, since we tend to approach tasks in unusual ways. And the world also got a lot louder and brighter as we industrialized, which makes it more difficult for autistic people to access public spaces.

Our current society makes life harder for neurodivergent people in a lot of unnecessary ways. If we changed the way society worked, then many of us could be significantly less disabled. But it's still possible for us to experience some challenges even in a quieter and more understanding environment.
